meta.title: Who really said "Eternity is a very long time, especially towards the end"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stephen Hawking — on camera in 2006 he credited Woody Allen. And Allen’s claim is unsourced: the joke appears in French print as early as 1965.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Eternity is a very long time, especially towards the end'?
meta.ogDescription: Hawking said it on CNN in 2006 — and credited Woody Allen in the same breath. Allen’s own claim has never been sourced.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — he was quoting Woody Allen
answer.authorDates: b. 1 December 1935 · American filmmaker, comedian and writer
answer.sourceLine: Hawking is credited with this because he is the one people heard say it. In a CNN Talk Asia interview broadcast on 4 July 2006 he used the line and attributed it in the same sentence — “as Woody Allen said.” That much is on the record. Whether it is Allen’s is a separate and unsettled question: Wikiquote has never been able to source it to him, and the joke turns up in French print two decades before anyone attached his name to it.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed. Hawking is ruled out by his own words. Woody Allen is the attribution Hawking gave and the one everyone repeats — but it has never been pinned to anything Allen wrote or performed.

source.heading: What is actually on the record

docMeta.dd: CNN “Talk Asia” interview with Stephen Hawking
“…as Woody Allen said” — he credited it, not claimed it
None located — Wikiquote lists it as unsourced

source.excerpt: We have long enough, as the universe should last for ever. Eternity is a very long time, especially towards the end, as Woody Allen said.
trail: The decisive evidence is Hawking’s own sentence. In the archived CNN “Talk Asia” transcript ↗ of 4 July 2006 he says: “We have long enough, as the universe should last for ever. Eternity is a very long time, especially towards the end, as Woody Allen said.” He is quoting, and he names his source.

Wikiquote’s Talk page for Hawking ↗ reaches the same conclusion and adds a useful negative: a 2007 Berkeley lecture often given as the origin has a published transcript that “doesn’t include the word ‘eternity’.”

Allen’s side is much weaker than its popularity suggests. The line sits in the Unsourced section of Wikiquote’s Talk page for Woody Allen ↗ and has never been promoted to his main quotations page ↗ — meaning no editor has ever produced a film, book, interview or routine containing it.

That Talk page also records printings that predate the Allen attribution entirely, in French: “l’éternité c’est long, surtout vers la fin” in Maurice Frot’s Le Roi des Rats (1965) and Pierre Henri Degrégori’s Le Temps de boules de neige (1969), neither crediting Allen. We were unable to inspect those two books ourselves, so we report them as that page’s research rather than as our own confirmation.
source.excerptNote: From the CNN “Talk Asia” transcript of 4 July 2006. The original cnn.com page is gone; we read the text in the Internet Archive’s capture ↗.
source.rightsNote: We cannot determine what work this line first appeared in, so we assert no rights status. Every candidate origin is modern — the earliest printing anyone has produced is 1965 — so it is certainly not in the United States public domain, which currently reaches published works through 1930. But with no identified source work and no established author, there is no identifiable rights holder either.

author.name: Woody Allen
author.heading: About Woody Allen
author.metaLine: b. 1 December 1935 · American filmmaker, comedian and writer
author.bio: Woody Allen, born Allen Stewart Königsberg in Brooklyn in 1935, began as a gag writer and stand-up comedian before turning to film. His comic register — mortality, God and the universe handled as material for a nightclub set — is exactly the register of this line, which is a large part of why the attribution to him has stuck so easily. It is worth being clear that fitting an author’s voice is not evidence, and in this case no source has ever been produced.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A rare case where the misattribution has an innocent cause: Hawking really did say it out loud, on camera, and gave credit that almost nobody repeated.

items.why: Refuted by Hawking himself. In the archived CNN transcript ↗ he ends the sentence “…as Woody Allen said.” The quotation survived; the four-word credit did not.

This is the best attribution available, and it is still weak. The line has never made it out of the Unsourced list on Allen’s Wikiquote Talk page ↗, and does not appear on his main page ↗ at all. No film, book or routine of his has been produced containing it.

Wikiquote editors found “l’éternité c’est long, surtout vers la fin” in a 1965 French novel and again in 1969, in neither case credited to Allen — who would have been in his twenties. See the Talk-page research ↗; we could not inspect the books directly.

misattribution.truthLine: Hawking gave the credit away in the same breath and it was lost anyway — and the man he gave it to may not be the author either. Read the transcript ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is doing real work in the interview, not just getting a laugh. Hawking has just argued that the universe created itself out of nothing under the laws of physics, and that we therefore have unlimited time to understand it completely. The joke is the deflation: unlimited time is not obviously a comfort.

It is also a small case study in how attribution decays. Hawking cited his source clearly and in public. The sentence was quotable and the credit was not, so within a few years the internet had reassigned the joke to the more striking speaker — a physicist in a wheelchair discussing eternity — and dropped the comedian entirely.
context.pull: The quotation survived. The credit did not.

sourcesVerified.claim: The archived CNN "Talk Asia" transcript of 4 July 2006 contains: "We have long enough, as the universe should last for ever. Eternity is a very long time, especially towards the end, as Woody Allen said." — read directly from the Internet Archive capture.

Wikiquote's Talk:Stephen Hawking page records that Hawking mentions the eternity line in the 2006 CNN Talk Asia transcript but attributes it to Woody Allen, notes this may itself be incorrect since it sits in the unsourced section for Allen, and observes that the Berkeley 2007 lecture transcript does not contain the word "eternity".

Wikiquote's Talk:Woody Allen page lists this line under its "Unsourced" heading, cites a 6 January 2001 British Medical Journal variant by Kevin Barraclough, and records French printings "l'eternite c'est long, surtout vers la fin" in Maurice Frot's Le Roi des Rats (1965) and Pierre Henri Degregori's Le Temps de boules de neige (1969) that do not credit Allen. Those two books were not inspected by us.
Wikiquote gives Woody Allen's birth as Allen Stewart Konigsberg, 1 December 1935, and its main Woody Allen page does NOT contain this quotation — checked by full-text search of the page source.
Wikiquote maintains a sourced quotations page for Stephen Hawking with a Misattributed section.
